children: New Delhi, Sept. 1 -- India is set to introduce polymer banknotes, starting with low-denominations, according to multiple reports. Indian and overseas companies are bidding to supply the specialised polymer substrate which is required to manufacture the notes, according to a report by The Indian Express. The development comes after Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Pvt Ltd (BRBNMPL), a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), invited global bids for polymer substrate sheets with built-in security features.

The latest report on the procurement also hints at the security concerns surrounding the production of Indian currency notes. Going by the same report, bidders have been required to sign an undertaking. It is described as a confidentiality agreement and a no-agent pact, declaring that their operations in India will be firewalled from any operations they may have in China and Pakistan. This condition suggests that while India is open to global suppliers, it is working to establish a separation between the Indian currency supply chain and the bidders' operations in its two neighbouring countries.

Earlier in July, an Expression of Interest (EOI) raised a requirement of 68,000 reams of BOPP (Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene)-based polymer substrate, 34,000 reams each for two denominations, each ream comprising 500 sheets, as per ANI.
Reportedly, these samples submitted by bidders will be tested across different climatic zones. Only those eligible will be allowed to make it to the final tender.
Applicants are also reportedly required to submit proof of net financial worth, manufacturing capacity, and eligibility for security clearance.

Among the companies reportedly in the race is Indian substrate manufacturer Cosmo First, which has partnered with UK-based banknote manufacturer De La Rue. The report added that Cosmo First has listed De La Rue as its technical partner, with the latter expected to provide security features for the polymer substrate. Australia's CCL Secure, which supplies polymer solutions to around 40 central banks, is another reported bidder who may supply polymer for Indian banknotes.
The final polymer substrate is expected to meet specific requirements.

The material must include security features, including a clear window with a portrait, a metallic numeral, a magnetic pseudo-thread, a shadow image, and an iridescent pattern, suitable for printing at the BRBNMPL and SPMCIL presses.

Apart from these requirements, bidders have been asked to certify that the material supplied to BRBNMPL contains no animal tallow or its DNA. Concerns over animal-derived materials in banknotes in countries such as the UK have been reported to be one reason behind the RBI's hesitation over polymer currency.
India's proposed transition to polymer notes is likely not to be an immediate replacement of the current paper currency.

The Indian Express also reported that the RBI is probably aiming for a combination of polymer and conventional cotton-based currency for the count, with Rs.10 and Rs.20 denominations likely becoming the first ones in polymer format. Polymer banknotes are marketed as more durable and secure than the traditional cotton-based notes. CCL Secure claimed that polymer notes can last six times longer than paper currency.

The government has not yet confirmed a full-scale rollout of polymer banknotes. Published by HT Digital Content Services with permission from MINT. For any query with respect to this article or any other content requirement, please contact Editor at contentservices@htdigital.in

title: India eyes plastic notes: How govt plans to keep polymer currency secure from China, Pakistan influence
